subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewer: Chee Skool Core Meaning refinement v1 review
reviewNotes: Post-research Core Meaning transfer set. Review ambiguity, distractor quality, answer balance, and learner timing before publish.

curriculum.learningObjective: Apply Core Meaning skills to a GED-length passage with close distractors and dispersed evidence.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the city begin by collecting measurements instead of immediately choosing one large construction project?

options.text: Officials had already decided to plant trees along the entire route.
options.whyWrong: Tree planting became one later test; it was not the reason the city began with measurements.

options.text: The city was required to wait several years before changing any bus stops.
options.whyWrong: No waiting requirement is stated.

options.text: Staff wanted to identify where pedestrians faced the greatest heat exposure before matching improvements to locations.
Residents asked the city to study air-conditioning use inside nearby apartments.
options.whyWrong: The passage focuses on pedestrian heat along the route, not apartment air-conditioning.

explanation.whyCorrect: The opening explains that staff wanted to know which parts of the route exposed pedestrians to the most heat before deciding what to change.
explanation.quickTip: Preserve the passage's stated reason instead of choosing a related project goal.
explanation.evidenceRef: City staff ... wanted to know which parts of the walking route exposed pedestrians to the most heat.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Reflective sidewalk coatings are the most effective way to reduce summer heat in every location.
options.whyWrong: The passage treats reflective surfaces as a supporting measure, not the best solution everywhere.

options.text: Young trees should not be used for heat reduction because they provide little shade during their first year.
options.whyWrong: It focuses on one early limitation of young trees and ignores their long-term role.

options.text: The city's main goal was to lower the neighborhood's overall air temperature with one treatment.
options.whyWrong: The project focused on pedestrian exposure and did not seek one treatment for overall air temperature.

options.text: Measurements helped the city see that different parts of the walking route needed different heat-reduction strategies, with shade playing an important but location-specific role.

explanation.whyCorrect: The passage moves from measurement to several pilot treatments and ends with a targeted plan rather than one universal solution.
explanation.quickTip: The best main idea should explain the measurement, testing, differences, and targeted planning.
explanation.evidenceRef: Instead of choosing one treatment for the entire route, staff proposed adding permanent shade first at waiting areas ... and planting new trees where long-term maintenance was realistic.

questions.prompt: Which detail provides the strongest support for the idea that shade changed the heat pedestrians experienced even when it did not greatly change local air temperature?

options.text: The shaded bus stop had similar nearby air temperature, but its bench and pavement stayed much cooler than uncovered surfaces.
Measurements were collected on twelve clear days in June and July.
options.whyWrong: This describes data collection but not the effect of shade.

options.text: The parking-lot crossing was one of the hottest parts of the route.
options.whyWrong: It identifies a hot location but does not compare shade with air temperature.

options.text: Young trees provided little benefit during the first summer.
options.whyWrong: It supports a point about tree maturity, not the immediate effect of shade.

explanation.whyCorrect: Choice A directly compares similar air temperature with cooler shaded surfaces, supporting both parts of the idea.
explanation.quickTip: For strongest-evidence questions, choose the detail that supports every important part of the target idea.
explanation.evidenceRef: The shaded bus stop was not dramatically cooler in the surrounding air, but the bench and pavement beneath the shelter stayed much cooler.

questions.prompt: Which choice best summarizes the paragraphs describing the three pilot changes and their results?

options.text: The city tested a canopy, young trees, and a lighter surface; each affected heat differently, showing that no single treatment worked the same way in every location.
The city planted trees because reflective surfaces and canopies failed to reduce heat.
options.whyWrong: The canopy and reflective surface did not fail.

options.text: The city tested three changes and found that all of them worked equally well, so officials planned to use all three everywhere.
options.whyWrong: The results were not identical and the city did not plan to use every treatment everywhere.

options.text: The city learned that young trees are useless during hot weather until they are fully mature.
options.whyWrong: It reduces the whole section to the first-summer limitation of young trees.

explanation.whyCorrect: The section compares three treatments and emphasizes that their effects differed.
explanation.quickTip: A section summary should keep the relationship among the details, not just one result.
explanation.evidenceRef: All three changes reduced surface heating under some conditions, but the results were not identical.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?

options.text: The city discovered that surface-temperature measurements are more useful than all other forms of heat research.
options.whyWrong: The passage never compares measurement methods this way.

options.text: A city pilot measured heat along a transit walk, tested several small interventions, and used the different results to plan targeted improvements rather than a single universal solution.
Residents asked the city to replace a hot parking lot with a tree-filled park, but underground utilities prevented the project.
options.whyWrong: This invents a park proposal and misstates the utility issue.

options.text: The project proved that permanent bus shelters are enough to solve pedestrian heat during summer.
options.whyWrong: The project did not eliminate summer heat or prove one complete solution.

explanation.whyCorrect: Choice B keeps the problem, measurement, pilot actions, different results, and final planning decision without overclaiming.
explanation.quickTip: A strong summary keeps the passage's main development and its limits.
explanation.evidenceRef: The measurements showed where pedestrians faced the greatest exposure and helped the city match different improvements to different parts of the walk.

questions.prompt: Which statement is directly supported about the lighter-colored surface coating?

options.text: It lowered the route's overall air temperature by the largest amount.
options.whyWrong: The passage does not say it lowered overall air temperature or was best.

options.text: It reduced midday surface temperature, but the area still felt uncomfortable because it remained in direct sun.
It made pedestrians report that the section was completely comfortable.
options.whyWrong: Pedestrians still reported discomfort.

options.text: It was installed only after the young trees had grown for several years.
options.whyWrong: The city planned to remeasure trees later; the coating was part of the initial pilot.

explanation.whyCorrect: The passage directly states both the lower surface temperature and continued discomfort from direct sun.
explanation.quickTip: Watch for answers that keep both the benefit and the limitation.
explanation.evidenceRef: The lighter coating reduced midday surface temperature, but pedestrians still reported discomfort because the section remained exposed to direct sun.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the city's decision not to use one heat-reduction treatment for the entire route?

options.text: Measurements were taken during June and July.
options.whyWrong: The measurement dates do not support the one-size-fits-all decision.

options.text: The route crossed wide intersections and a parking lot.
options.whyWrong: This explains why the route can feel hot but not why one treatment was rejected.

options.text: The three tested changes produced different kinds and amounts of benefit under different conditions.
The city planned to repeat measurements after the trees grew.
options.whyWrong: Future monitoring matters, but it does not directly explain why the plan uses different treatments.

explanation.whyCorrect: Different results across conditions directly support matching different treatments to different locations.
explanation.quickTip: Choose evidence that explains the decision itself, not just project background.
explanation.evidenceRef: All three changes reduced surface heating under some conditions, but the results were not identical.

title: Cooling the Walk to Transit
